etymology: Two unrelated words share the spelling. The noun boss, a master or employer, is American from the seventeenth century, from Dutch baas (master) in New Amsterdam. The adjective boss, "excellent, first-rate," grew out of it: it is recorded in nineteenth-century American slang and was revived in the 1950s–60s among Black and teenage speakers ("that car is boss"); Los Angeles station KHJ branded itself "Boss Radio" in 1965. The 1828 boss — a stud or knob, from French bosse — is a third, older word (see bosses).
biblical_def: In Boomer slang, boss means excellent, the best, top of the heap: "That’s a boss Mustang." The word borrows the glory of the man in charge and pins it on whatever is admired. The Christian observation: the slang quietly assumes that being the boss is the highest thing — that to call something "boss" is to give it the top rank. The Lord Jesus turned that assumption over. When His disciples argued about who would be greatest, He said, "whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister; And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant: Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Mat 20:26–28). In His kingdom the boss is the one who serves. Paul tells earthly masters to remember that they too are under authority: "Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven" (Col 4:1). And the Lord says flatly, "one is your Master, even Christ" (Mat 23:10). So a Christian can enjoy the word — a car can be boss, a guitar riff can be boss — while teaching his children where true excellence lives. The truly boss thing in the universe is a King who washed His servants’ feet.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (19th c., revived 1950s–60s) for excellent, first-rate, from boss (master) — a word that crowns being in charge, which Christ redefined: "whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant" (Mat 20:27).
webster_full: BOSS, adj. (Boomer slang, 1950s–60s; earlier 19th-c. American) Excellent, outstanding, first-rate. "That’s a boss car." "Boss Radio." From boss, n., a master or employer (Dutch baas).
Note: the 1828 boss (a knob or stud) is a different word from French bosse, a swelling — see bosses (Job 15:26).
Decode for families: Gen Z’s nearest equivalents are fire, goated, elite.
scriptures: But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant:
Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
Col 4:1
Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.
Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even Christ.
corruption_summary: The slang crowns whatever is admired with the title of the man in charge; Christ crowns the servant, and reminds every master that he has a Master in heaven.
corruption_paragraphs: Language reveals what a culture admires, and boss reveals a lot. The best thing you can say about a car or a song is that it is like the man who gives orders. That is the world’s ranking, and the disciples shared it until the night before the cross, when they were still arguing about rank at the Lord’s Supper. The gospel does not abolish authority — masters and servants, parents and children, elders and congregations all remain — but it relocates greatness. The greatest in the kingdom is the one who serves (Mat 20:26).

For a father, the word is an opportunity. In your household you are, in a real sense, the boss. Scripture asks you to be the kind of boss Col 4:1 describes — just and equal, knowing you answer to a Master in heaven — and the kind Mat 20:28 embodies, giving yourself for those under you. A son who sees that will learn what boss really means.
roots_summary: Dutch baas (master) → American boss (17th c.) → adj. boss (excellent, 19th c.; revived 1950s–60s); distinct from 1828 boss (knob, French bosse).
roots_lines: Dutch baas — master, foreman; borrowed in New Amsterdam (17th c.)
American English: boss — employer, overseer; political boss (19th c.)
19th c., revived 1950s–60s: boss (adj.) — excellent, first-rate
1965: KHJ Los Angeles, "Boss Radio"
Separate word: French bosse — a swelling, a knob; 1828 BOSS, a stud (see Bosses)
usage: "Grandpa’s ’67 Chevelle is boss." "It sure is — and he still changes his own oil."
Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant (Mat 20:27).
Ye also have a Master in heaven (Col 4:1).

etymology: From French net (clean, pure), Latin nitidus (shining). The older English senses — clean, tidy, pure, unmixed ("whiskey neat") — are centuries old and are those Webster gave in 1828. The slang sense — excellent, wonderful, "cool" — is American and recorded from the 1930s; it became the signature word of 1950s and early-1960s kids ("Gee, that’s neat!", "neat-o"), the Leave It to Beaver generation, and remains the gentlest compliment in the Boomer vocabulary.
biblical_def: To a Boomer kid of 1958, neat meant wonderful: a new bike, a model rocket, a trip to the drive-in — "Gee, Wally, that’s neat." It is still the word a grandparent reaches for when a grandchild shows him something. The Christian observation: the slang sense grew out of an older, richer one, and the older one is worth recovering. In 1828 neat meant very clean, pure, free from what does not belong, well-ordered — and those are qualities Scripture commends. "Let all things be done decently and in order" (1Co 14:40). God Himself works neatly: "He hath made every thing beautiful in his time" (Ecc 3:11), and at the end of creation "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good" (Gen 1:31). The Boomer use of neat for "delightful" preserves a small truth: there is a pleasure in things that are well made, clean, and fitted to their purpose. That pleasure is a reflection of God’s own delight in His works. A grandfather who says "neat" about a child’s drawing is doing something godly in a modest way — delighting in a creature’s work. The Christian can go one step further and teach the child to think on "whatsoever things are lovely" (Php 4:8) and to give thanks to the One who made the world so full of neat things.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (from 1930s American; signature 1950s–60s kid word) for wonderful, excellent — grown from the 1828 sense of clean, pure, well-ordered, which echoes the God who made every thing beautiful in his time (Ecc 3:11).
webster_full: NEAT, adj. (American slang, 1930s; Boomer staple 1950s–60s) Excellent, wonderful, delightful. "That’s neat!" Also neat-o, neato.

Webster (1828) — NEAT, adjective [Latin to shine, to be clean, fair or fine; pure, to purify, to winnow.] 1. Very clean; free from foul or extraneous matter; as neat clothes. The vessels are kept neat; the woman keeps her house very neat 2. Pure; free from impure words and phrases; as a neat style. 3. Cleanly; preserving neatness; as a neat woman. 4. Pure; unadulterated; as neat wine. 5. Free from tawdry appendages and well adjusted; as a neat dress.
Decode for families: the slang survives in every generation; the 1828 sense survives in "keep your room neat."
scriptures: Gen 1:31
And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.
Ecc 3:11
He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
corruption_summary: A wholesome word; the only loss is that its older sense — clean, pure, ordered — has faded behind the newer "nice," and Scripture invites us to recover both.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in neat, only something to recover. The word moved from describing a quality of things (clean, ordered, unmixed) to describing a reaction to things (I like it). That shift is typical of modern English: words that once named what is true about the world now name how we feel about it. Scripture keeps both. God saw that creation was good — a fact — and He took delight in it — a response.

A Christian family can use the word in both senses on purpose. A neat room is an ordered one, and order is a reflection of the God who is not the author of confusion (1Co 14:40 stands in the same chapter). A neat sunset is a delight, and delight is the right response to a beautiful thing that God has made in His time (Ecc 3:11).
roots_summary: Latin nitidus (shining) → French net (clean) → English neat (clean, tidy, pure) → 1930s American slang (excellent) → 1950s–60s Boomer kid word.
roots_lines: Latin nitere, nitidus — to shine; shining, bright
Old French net — clean, pure (compare English net, after deductions)
16th c.–: neat — clean, tidy; pure, unmixed (neat spirits)
1930s American slang: neat — excellent, fine
1950s–60s: the signature compliment of Boomer childhood; neat-o
usage: "Grandpa looked at my science project and said, ‘Now that’s neat.’ Best review I got."
He hath made every thing beautiful in his time (Ecc 3:11).
Let all things be done decently and in order (1Co 14:40).

etymology: From Italian and Spanish primo, "first" (Latin primus). As American slang for first-rate, top-quality, the best of its kind, primo spread in the 1970s, partly through Spanish-speaking communities in the Southwest and California and partly through the drug trade, where primo marked the best-grade marijuana; it soon broadened to anything excellent ("primo seats," "a primo wave").
biblical_def: Primo means first-rate, top-shelf, the best available: primo seats at the ballgame, a primo parking spot, a primo surf break. The word is literally "first." The Christian observation: Scripture has a great deal to say about what comes first, and it reorders our list. "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you" (Mat 6:33). The primo thing in a believer’s life is not a seat or a parking spot but the reign of God. Christ Himself is the true Primo: "he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence" (Col 1:18), and He says, "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last" (Rev 22:13). Israel was taught to give God the primo portion of everything: "The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the LORD thy God" (Exo 23:19); "Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase" (Pro 3:9). The habit the word suggests — grabbing the best for oneself — is the habit Scripture reverses: the best goes to God first, and the Christian takes the lower seat at the feast. Teach a child to give God the primo, and to let others have the primo seat.
webster_summary: Boomer-era slang (1970s, from Spanish / Italian primo, "first") for top-quality, first-rate — a word Scripture turns toward the One who must have the preeminence (Col 1:18) and the firstfruits given to God (Pro 3:9).
webster_full: PRIMO, adj. (American slang, 1970s–present) First-rate, top-quality, excellent. "We got primo seats." Originally also of high-grade marijuana.

Webster (1828) — PRIME, adjective [Latin primus.] 1. First in order of time; original; as prime fathers; prime creation. In this sense, the use of the word is nearly superseded by primitive, except in the phrase, prime cost. 2. First in rank, degree or dignity; as prime minister. 3. First in excellence; as prime wheat; cloth of a prime quality. Humility and resignation are prime virtues.
Decode for families: in a teenager’s mouth today it is usually innocent; in a 1970s context it may refer to drugs.
scriptures: Mat 6:33
But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.
The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the LORD thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.
Pro 3:9
Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:
corruption_summary: Primo trains the eye to grab the best for oneself; Scripture gives the first and best to God and teaches the believer to take the lower seat.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is harmless, but the instinct behind it deserves a look. Primo is about getting the best — the best seat, spot, grade, deal. Our Lord watched guests at a feast doing exactly that, choosing the chief rooms, and told them to take the lowest place instead, "For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased." The Christian does not despise good things; he simply does not grab them.

The deeper reordering is in worship. Israel’s firstfruits law meant that the first sheaf, the first lamb, the first coin belonged to God before anything belonged to the family. That is not stinginess about the rest; it is a confession about who comes first. A household that gives God the primo portion — of its income, its week, its attention — is living Mat 6:33 in the most concrete way.
roots_lines: Latin primus — first, foremost, chief
Italian / Spanish primo — first; (Spanish) also cousin
English prime — first in rank, excellence, or time (1828 PRIME)
1970s American slang: primo — top-quality; also high-grade marijuana
Greek prōteuō — to have the preeminence (Col 1:18)
usage: "Grandpa got primo seats behind home plate and spent the whole game explaining the infield fly rule."
Seek ye first the kingdom of God (Mat 6:33).
That in all things he might have the preeminence (Col 1:18).

etymology: From Latin decens, present participle of decere, "to be fitting." The standard senses — becoming, proper, respectable, modest — are old (Webster 1828: "becoming; fit; suitable"). Two slang senses belong to the Boomer era: decent as "pretty good, satisfactory, cool" (1960s–70s teen use: "that’s decent"), and are you decent?, "are you dressed?", said before entering a room (mid-twentieth century). The first was picked up again by later surfers and Gen X.
biblical_def: In Boomer slang decent means pretty good, acceptable, not bad: "That burger was decent." It is praise with a shrug. Older meanings still live underneath: a decent person is respectable and honest; to be decent is to be properly clothed. The Christian observation: the word is a good place to ask how high we aim. The slang sense sets the bar at "good enough." Scripture does not. "Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect" (Mat 5:48). A merely decent faith is what the Lord rebuked in Laodicea: "because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth" (Rev 3:16). Many Boomers grew up in churches full of decent people — respectable, upright, unexceptional — and some concluded that Christianity was simply decency with hymns. It is not. The gospel is not for decent people; it is for sinners, and it makes them saints. Yet the older sense of decent is a real virtue, and Scripture commends it: "Let all things be done decently and in order" (1Co 14:40); "Let us walk honestly, as in the day" (Rom 13:13); women adorned "in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9). Decency in that sense — propriety, modesty, honesty — is the outward fruit of an inward grace. Aim at holiness, and decency will come along; aim only at decency, and you will miss both.
webster_summary: Boomer slang for "pretty good, acceptable" (also are you decent? = dressed) on the 1828 root "becoming, fit" — a modest virtue Scripture commends (1Co 14:40) but never accepts as the aim in place of holiness (Mat 5:48).
webster_full: DECENT, adj. (Boomer slang senses, mid-20th c.–present) 1. Fairly good; satisfactory; cool ("a decent burger"). 2. Properly clothed: "Are you decent?"

Webster (1828) — DECENT, adjective [Latin decens; Fr. decent ] 1. Becoming; fit; suitable, in words, behavior, dress and ceremony; as decent language; decent conduct or actions; decent ornaments or dress. 2. Comely; not gaudy or ostentatious. A sable stole of Cyprus lawn O’er the decent shoulders drawn. 3. Not immodest.
Decode for families: "decent" as praise is faint praise. "Decent" as character — honest, modest, upright — is high praise.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
Mat 5:48
Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.
Rev 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
corruption_summary: The slang sets the bar at "good enough," and mid-century churchgoing often confused the gospel with respectability; Scripture commends decency as fruit but demands holiness as the aim.
corruption_paragraphs: Decent is the moral vocabulary of respectability: decent folks, a decent neighborhood, a decent living. The Boomers inherited a culture that prized it and saw, rightly, how often it covered hypocrisy and indifference. Their mistake was to throw out decency itself. Our Lord’s complaint against the respectable was never that they were too modest or too honest; it was that their decency was all outside, "whited sepulchres." The cure for whitewash is not dirt.

Scripture keeps decency in its place. It is real and commanded (1Co 14:40; Rom 13:13), but it is not righteousness. "Except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees," the Lord said — and they were the most decent men in Jerusalem. Only Christ’s righteousness, given to sinners, exceeds theirs. A father can teach his son: be decent, always; but never think decency will save you.
roots_summary: Latin decere (to be fitting) → decens → English decent (becoming, proper, modest) → mid-20th-c. slang: "dressed"; "pretty good."
roots_lines: Latin decere — to be fitting, to become; decorum, propriety
16th c.–: decent — becoming, suitable, proper; modest
Mid-20th c.: Are you decent? — Are you dressed?
1960s–70s teen slang: decent — good, satisfactory, cool
Greek euschēmonōs — decently, becomingly (1Co 14:40; Rom 13:13)
usage: "How was the sermon?" "Decent." "Son, the sermon was fine. Was your listening decent?"
Let all things be done decently and in order (1Co 14:40).
Be ye therefore perfect (Mat 5:48) — decency is the floor, not the ceiling.

etymology: Clipped from fabulous (Latin fabulosus, celebrated in fable). Fab is British slang of the early 1960s, made world-famous by the Beatles, whom the Liverpool press and their press officer Tony Barrow dubbed "the Fab Four" in 1963; with Beatlemania it crossed to America in February 1964. It meant terrific, marvelous, and carried the whole bright, mop-topped optimism of 1964–65. It enjoyed a second life in the 1990s and 2000s (Queer Eye’s "Fab Five," 2003).
biblical_def: Fab is short for fabulous — marvelous, terrific, wonderful — and to Boomers it will forever mean the Beatles, the Fab Four, and the moment in February 1964 when seventy-three million Americans watched them on The Ed Sullivan Show. The Christian observation: the word’s root is worth a moment. Fabulous first meant "belonging to fable" — legendary, not real. Beatlemania was fabulous in both senses: marvelous, and built on a kind of legend, as screaming crowds made four young musicians into something like gods. John Lennon said as much in 1966, telling a London reporter that the Beatles were "more popular than Jesus now," and records were burned across the American South when the remark was reprinted. Whatever Lennon meant, the observation exposed something true about celebrity. Scripture records what happens when a crowd treats a man as divine: when Herod spoke, "the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man. And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory" (Act 12:22–23). "Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm" (Jer 17:5). John’s closing words are the right word to every fan: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (1Jn 5:21). The music can be enjoyed; the musicians can be admired; but the truly fabulous — the marvelous that is no fable — is the gospel, which Peter insisted was not "cunningly devised fables" but eyewitness truth.
webster_summary: Early-1960s British slang (clipped fabulous) made famous by the Beatles, "the Fab Four" (1963) — a reminder that celebrity can become idolatry (Act 12:22–23; 1Jn 5:21), and that the true marvel is the gospel, which is no fable.
webster_full: FAB, adj. (British slang, early 1960s; Boomer era) Fabulous; terrific; wonderful. "The Fab Four" — the Beatles (1963).

Webster (1828) — FABULOUS, adjective 1. Feigned, as a story; devised; fictitious; as a fabulous story; a fabulous description. 2. Related in fable; described or celebrated in fables; invented; not real; as a fabulous hero; the fabulous exploits of Hercules. 3. The fabulous age of Greece and Rome, was the early age of those countries, the accounts of which are mostly fabulous or in which the fabulous achievements of their heroes were performed; called also the heroic age.
Decode for families: fabulous once meant "fabled, unreal." Peter used the contrast: "we have not followed cunningly devised fables" (2Pe 1:16).
scriptures: And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.
And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.
Jer 17:5
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.
Exo 20:3
Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
corruption_summary: Fab carried the joy of Beatlemania and also its idolatry of celebrity; Scripture warns against giving men the glory due to God and calls the gospel the one marvel that is no fable.
corruption_paragraphs: Beatlemania was something new: a mass devotion, mostly of teenage girls, expressed in screaming, fainting, and a kind of worship. The word fab was its liturgy. Older generations had their idols too — Sinatra had bobby-soxers — but television made the scale unprecedented, and the pattern has repeated with every pop phenomenon since. Lennon’s 1966 remark was arrogant, but it was also, sadly, a fair report on where the devotion of many young people had gone.

The Christian answer is not record-burning; it is the first commandment (Exo 20:3) taught with joy. Music is a gift, and the Beatles wrote some fine songs. But no performer can bear the weight of worship, and many have been crushed under it. The gospel offers what celebrity promises and cannot give: a glory that is real, a Person worthy of all devotion, and a marvel that is history, not fable.
roots_summary: Latin fabula (a story) → fabulosus → English fabulous (fabled; then marvelous) → early-1960s British clip fab → 1963 "the Fab Four."
roots_lines: Latin fabula — a story, a fable; fabulosus — celebrated in story
English fabulous — fabled, legendary (1828); later, marvelous, incredible
Early 1960s British slang: fab
1963: the Beatles dubbed "the Fab Four"; February 9, 1964, The Ed Sullivan Show
March 1966: Lennon’s "more popular than Jesus" remark (London Evening Standard)
usage: "Grandma still calls anything she likes ‘fab.’ She saw the Beatles at Shea Stadium in 1965 and can’t remember a single song for the screaming."
It is the voice of a god, and not of a man (Act 12:22) — the crowd’s error in every age.
Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1Jn 5:21).

etymology: Gear (Old Norse gervi, apparel; Middle English gere, equipment, dress) is an old noun for equipment, clothing, and harness; Webster gives it in 1828. As an adjective meaning excellent, great, gear is Liverpool and Merseyside slang of the early 1960s, carried worldwide by the Beatles and their fans in 1963–65 ("That’s gear!"). In the 1960s London fashion scene, gear also meant fashionable clothes. In later drug slang it meant narcotics.
biblical_def: In the Beatles’ Liverpool, gear meant great, terrific: "That song’s gear." In Carnaby Street it meant fashionable clothes: "Where’d you get that gear?" The Christian observation: the slang adjective came and went, but the noun underneath it — gear as clothing and equipment — is one of Scripture’s favorite images for the Christian life. The believer is told what gear to put on. "Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil" (Eph 6:11). "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering" (Col 3:12). "Be clothed with humility" (1Pe 5:5). And above all, "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof" (Rom 13:14). The 1960s mod in his fashionable gear was dressing for the gaze of others. The Christian dresses, in this deeper sense, for battle and for service, and his outfit is a Person. A father can tell his son, as the boy pulls on his gear for football or hunting, that every morning there is better gear to put on, and that no one goes out the door well-dressed without it.
webster_summary: Early-1960s Liverpool slang (Beatles era) for excellent; also fashionable clothes — on the 1828 root gear, dress and equipment, which Scripture fills with the whole armour of God (Eph 6:11) and the putting on of Christ (Rom 13:14).
webster_full: GEAR, adj. (Liverpool slang, early 1960s; Beatles era) Excellent, great. "That’s gear." n. (1960s London) Fashionable clothes. Later drug slang: narcotics.

Webster (1828) — GEAR, noun 1. Apparatus; whatever is prepared; hence, habit; dress; ornaments. Array thyself in her most gorgeous gear 2. More generally, the harness or furniture of beasts; whatever is used in equipping horses or cattle for draught; tackle. 3. In Scotland, warlike accouterments; also, goods, riches.
Decode for families: the adjective is dead; the noun is alive in every sports bag.
scriptures: Eph 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Col 3:12
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
corruption_summary: Gear moved from equipment to fashion to praise; the danger is dressing for the gaze of others, which Scripture answers by telling the believer what to put on.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1960s London scene that gave us gear for clothes was the first great youth-fashion market: Carnaby Street, Mary Quant, the mod suit and the miniskirt. Young people learned that identity could be bought and worn, and that what you wore announced who you were. That lesson has only intensified. Scripture does not forbid clothes or care; it forbids making them the self (1Pe 3:3).

The New Testament’s wardrobe is moral and spiritual. Paul lists it in Col 3:12 — mercies, kindness, humbleness, meekness, longsuffering — and in Eph 6 — truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the Word. That is the gear that does not go out of style. And Rom 13:14 sums it up: the believer is clothed with Christ.
roots_summary: Old Norse gervi (apparel) → Middle English gere (equipment, dress) → English gear → early-1960s Liverpool adj. gear (great) → 1960s London "fashionable clothes."
roots_lines: Old Norse gervi, görvi — apparel, equipment
Middle English gere — equipment, armour, dress, goods
1828: GEAR — dress, ornaments; harness; apparatus
Early 1960s Merseyside slang: gear (adj.) — excellent; spread by Beatlemania
Greek panoplia — the whole armour (Eph 6:11)
usage: "Grandma says in 1964 all her friends said ‘gear’ because Paul McCartney did."
Put on the whole armour of God (Eph 6:11).
Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ (Rom 13:14) — the best gear there is.

etymology: From Old English tóh, firm, tenacious. The ordinary senses — strong, hard to break or chew, difficult, rough — are old (Webster 1828). As teen slang of the 1950s and early 1960s, tough also meant excellent, sharp, impressive ("a tough car," "tough threads"), especially in the greaser and hot-rod culture; alongside it ran tough as an insult for a hoodlum ("a bunch of toughs") and the dismissive tough luck / tough!
biblical_def: In 1950s and 60s teen slang, tough meant sharp, cool, impressive: a tough car, a tough jacket. It also named a kind of young man — the greaser in the leather jacket, the tough guy who did not cry. The Christian observation: Scripture wants men to be tough, but in a different way and for a different reason. Paul writes, "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2Ti 2:3), and "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong" (1Co 16:13). God told Joshua, "Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest" (Jos 1:9). That is real toughness: endurance, courage, standing fast. But the world’s tough guy is often brittle — hard on the outside to protect what is fragile inside, unable to weep, to confess, or to be gentle. Scripture’s strong man is also tender: "be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you" (Eph 4:32). And his toughness does not come from himself: "when I am weak, then am I strong" (2Co 12:10). The toughest Man who ever lived set His face toward Jerusalem knowing what waited, and also took children in His arms. A father who wants a tough son should show him both.
webster_summary: 1950s–60s teen slang for sharp, impressive, cool — on the 1828 root "firm, tenacious" — a toughness Scripture commands (2Ti 2:3; 1Co 16:13) but joins to tenderness (Eph 4:32) and to strength made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:10).
webster_full: TOUGH, adj. (Boomer teen slang, 1950s–60s) Excellent, sharp, impressive. "That’s a tough car." n. A rough, aggressive young man; a hoodlum. Tough luck! / Tough! — too bad.

Webster (1828) — TOUGH, adjective tuf. 1. Having the quality of flexibility without brittleness; yielding to force without breaking. The ligaments of animals and of India rubber are remarkably tough tough timber, like young ash, is the most proper for the shafts and springs of a carriage. 2. Firm; strong; not easily broken; able to endure hardship; as an animal of a tough frame. 3. Not easily separated; viscous; clammy; tenacious; ropy; as tough phlegm. 4. Stiff; not flexible.
Decode for families: the greaser’s "tough" is the ancestor of every later word that praises hardness — badass, savage, alpha.
scriptures: Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Jos 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.
Eph 4:32
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
corruption_summary: The tough-guy ideal prizes hardness and hides weakness; Scripture commands endurance and courage but roots them in God’s strength and joins them to a tender heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1950s tough — James Dean, Marlon Brando, the leather-jacketed greaser — was a rebel against suburban softness, and there was something right in the protest. A culture that produces men who cannot endure hardness is in trouble. But the tough-guy image confused toughness with coldness. It taught boys that strength means never needing anyone, never admitting fault, never showing grief. That is not strength; it is armor over a wound, and it breaks marriages.

The biblical man is tougher than the greaser and softer than the suburbanite. He endures hardness as a soldier (2Ti 2:3) and weeps at a friend’s grave. He stands fast in the faith (1Co 16:13) and forgives as he has been forgiven (Eph 4:32). And he knows his strength is borrowed: "when I am weak, then am I strong" (2Co 12:10). That is the only toughness that lasts past forty.
roots_summary: Old English tóh (tenacious, firm) → English tough (strong, hard, difficult) → 1950s–60s teen slang tough (excellent, sharp); a tough (a hoodlum).
roots_lines: Old English tóh — tenacious, sticky, firm
English tough — strong, not easily broken; hard to chew; difficult
19th c.: a tough — a rough, a ruffian
1950s–60s greaser and hot-rod slang: tough — excellent, sharp
Greek krataioō — to be strong (1Co 16:13); kakopatheō — to endure hardship (2Ti 2:3)
usage: "Grandpa says his ’57 Bel Air was tough. Grandma says he was the one who thought he was tough."
Endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ (2Ti 2:3).
Be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted (Eph 4:32) — the other half of toughness.

etymology: From cherry, the fruit (Old North French cherise, Latin cerasum), whose bright red, unblemished skin made it a byword for fresh perfection. In 1950s–60s American car culture cherry meant in mint, original, flawless condition ("a cherry ’57 Chevy"), and the word is still standard among collectors of cars, guitars, and comics. (The word also has a crude slang sense among teenagers; context usually makes the car-lot meaning plain.)
biblical_def: To a Boomer car man, cherry is the highest praise: a vehicle in perfect, original condition, no rust, no dents, everything as it came from the factory. "He’s got a cherry ’66 Mustang in the garage." The Christian observation: the word expresses a real longing — for something unspoiled, perfect, preserved from decay — and every collector knows how hard that is to keep. Moth and rust get everything eventually. The Lord Jesus said exactly that: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt" (Mat 6:19–20). The only truly cherry possession is the one Peter describes: "an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you" (1Pe 1:4). And there is a cherry condition God intends for His people. Christ gave Himself for the church "That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish" (Eph 5:27). James calls believers to keep themselves "unspotted from the world" (Jas 1:27). A grandfather who spends his Saturdays keeping a car cherry can teach a grandson something lasting: it takes constant care to keep anything from corruption, and the soul is worth more care than the car.
webster_summary: 1950s–60s car-culture slang for mint, original, flawless condition — a longing for the unspoiled that only the inheritance incorruptible fulfils (1Pe 1:4), and the spotless church Christ is preparing (Eph 5:27).
webster_full: CHERRY, adj. (American car slang, 1950s–60s; Boomer era) In perfect, original, unblemished condition. "A cherry ’57 Chevy." Still standard among collectors.

Webster (1828) — CHERRY, noun The fruit of a tree, a species of Prunus, of which there are many varieties, as the red or garden cherry the red heart, the white heart, the black cherry the black heart, and several others. The fruit is a pulp inclosing a kernel. It is related that this fruit was brought from Cerasus in Pontus to Italy, after the defeat of Mithridates by Lucullus, A R. 680., and introduced into England by the Romans, about 120 years afterwards, adjective D. 55. Barbadoes cherry is the genus Malpighia, of several species. The berries are red, cherry-shaped, acid and eatable. Bird cherry is a species of Prunus, the common laurel or lauro-cerasus. Also, the Prunus padus. Cornelian cherry is the fruit of the Cornus, cornel-tree or dogwood. It is a small, acid, cherry-like, eatable berry. Dwarf cherry is the fruit of a species of Lonicera, or honey-suckle.
Decode for families: among teens the word has a crude second meaning. Grandpa almost certainly means the car.
scriptures: Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,
Eph 5:27
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: The car man’s cherry is a harmless delight that can become a treasure laid up where moth and rust corrupt; Scripture points the longing for the unspoiled to an inheritance incorruptible.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with a man keeping a beautiful machine in beautiful condition. Craftsmanship and care are good, and a restored car can be a fine thing to share with a grandson. The danger is the one Our Lord named: treasure on earth (Mat 6:19). The garage can become a shrine, the car an idol, and the Saturday polish a liturgy. Every collector knows the anxiety of the first scratch.

Scripture redirects the longing rather than mocking it. The desire for something perfect and preserved is a desire for heaven. Peter’s description of the believer’s inheritance reads like a collector’s dream — incorruptible, undefiled, unfading, kept safe (1Pe 1:4). And the one thing on earth God is keeping cherry is His church, washed and presented without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27).
roots_summary: Greek kerasos → Latin cerasum → Old North French cherise → English cherry (misread as plural) → 1950s–60s car slang (mint condition).
roots_lines: Greek kerasos — the cherry tree
Latin cerasum → Old North French cherise
Middle English cheri — back-formed, as if cherise were a plural
1950s–60s American car culture: cherry — mint, original condition
Greek aphthartos — incorruptible (1Pe 1:4)
usage: "Grandpa’s truck is cherry. He says the trick is a little care every single week."
Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt (Mat 6:20).
An inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away (1Pe 1:4).

etymology: The catchphrase of James "J.J." Evans Jr., played by Jimmie Walker on the CBS sitcom Good Times (1974–79), drawn out as "DY-NO-MITE!" with arms flung wide. Walker said it was the show’s director, John Rich, who pressed him to make it a weekly line. It became one of the most imitated catchphrases of the 1970s, on T-shirts, posters, and playgrounds. From dynamite (Alfred Nobel, 1867, from Greek dynamis, power), already slang for "excellent" (see Dynamite).
biblical_def: Dy-no-mite! was J.J.’s exclamation of triumph on Good Times: something is fantastic, terrific, explosive. Every Boomer and many of their children shouted it in the 1970s. The Christian observation: the word underneath is dynamite, and dynamite is named for the Greek dynamis, power — the very word Paul uses for the gospel: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth" (Rom 1:16). Preachers love that connection, and it is a good one so long as we remember the direction of borrowing: Nobel named his explosive after the Greek word, not the other way round, and the gospel’s power is not destructive but life-giving. Paul says his preaching came "not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power: That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God" (1Co 2:4–5). The catchphrase itself was joy, and joy is no small thing in a family. Good Times was set in a Chicago housing project, and J.J.’s exuberance lit up a hard life. "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22). The Christian can laugh at J.J. with a clear conscience and then show a child the real dynamite: a message that raises the dead.
webster_summary: 1970s TV catchphrase (J.J. Evans, Good Times, 1974–79) for "terrific!" — built on dynamite, from Greek dynamis, the "power of God unto salvation" (Rom 1:16), which gives life rather than destroying it.
webster_full: DY-NO-MITE!, interj. (1970s TV catchphrase; Boomer era) Terrific! Fantastic! From J.J. Evans (Jimmie Walker), Good Times, CBS, 1974–79.
From dynamite (Alfred Nobel, 1867; Greek dynamis, power), slang for excellent (see Dynamite).
Decode for families: say it with arms wide and a three-beat pause; your grandparents will laugh.
scriptures: Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
corruption_summary: A joyful, harmless catchphrase; its root word, dynamis, points to the gospel as the power of God unto salvation — power that gives life rather than destroys.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct here. J.J.’s catchphrase was clean, exuberant, and funny, and it gave a hard-pressed family on television a moment of joy each week. If anything, it reminds us how much a merry heart matters (Pro 17:22) in a home under strain. The only caution is the usual one about any catchphrase: it can become a substitute for real speech, a way of performing enthusiasm rather than feeling it.

The word’s root is the treasure. Dynamis is the power the risen Christ promised: "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you" (Act 1:8). That power did not blow anything up; it built a church out of fishermen. A father can tell his son that the real dynamite in the world is not in a stick but in a sentence: Christ died for our sins, and rose again the third day.
roots_lines: Greek dynamis — power, might, miraculous power (Rom 1:16; Act 1:8)
1867: Alfred Nobel names his explosive dynamite
20th c.: dynamite (adj.) — excellent, powerful (see Dynamite)
1974–79: Good Times, CBS; Jimmie Walker as J.J. — "DY-NO-MITE!"
1970s: printed on T-shirts and posters; a national playground shout
usage: "When I got an A in chemistry, Grandpa threw his arms out and yelled, ‘Dy-no-mite!’"
The gospel of Christ is the power (dynamis) of God unto salvation (Rom 1:16).
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine (Pro 17:22).

etymology: Short for modern or modernist, originally the London youths of the late 1950s who loved modern jazz. By the early 1960s the Mods were a British subculture of sharp tailored suits, parkas, Italian scooters, soul and R&B, and pills, famous for their seaside brawls with the leather-clad Rockers at Clacton, Margate, and Brighton in 1964; the Who were their band. In America mod came to mean the whole "Swinging London" look of 1965–67 — Carnaby Street, Mary Quant’s miniskirt, Twiggy, op-art prints.
biblical_def: A Mod was a fashion-obsessed British youth of the early 1960s — immaculate suits, scooters with a dozen mirrors, all-night dancing — and in America mod meant anything in the Swinging London style: miniskirts, geometric prints, white boots. "That dress is so mod." The Christian observation: the Mod subculture made fashion a religion of the young, and its rivalry with the Rockers made it a tribe. Both are old temptations. Paul writes, "Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26) — a fair description of two gangs of teenagers fighting on Brighton beach over hairstyles and music. The deeper issue is identity. The Mod was what he wore. Scripture locates a person’s worth elsewhere: "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart" (1Pe 3:3–4). And the mod style’s most famous product, the miniskirt, raises a question every Christian family still faces: Paul’s call for "modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9). The 1828 word modest sits right beside mod in the dictionary, and the two make a useful pair: one is what the world calls up to date, the other what God calls becoming. "Be not conformed to this world" (Rom 12:2) does not require looking old-fashioned; it requires that fashion never sit on the throne.
webster_summary: Early-1960s British youth subculture (from modern) of sharp suits, scooters, and soul; in America, the Swinging London style of 1965–67 — fashion as identity and tribe, set by Scripture against the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4) and modest apparel (1Ti 2:9).
webster_full: MOD, n. (British, late 1950s–60s; Boomer era) A member of a youth subculture devoted to sharp modern fashion, scooters, and soul / R&B music, rivals of the Rockers. adj. (US, 1965–67) In the bold, youthful London style; fashionable, up to date. "A mod dress."

Webster (1828) — MODERN, adjective [Latin modo, and ern, which we find in other Latin words that have reference to time, as in hodiernus, hesternus.] 1. Pertaining to the present time, or time not long past; late; recent; not ancient or remote in past time; as modern days, ages or time; modern authors; modern fashions; modern taste; modern practice. 2. Common; mean; vulgar. [ Not used .]
Decode for families: mod and modest share nothing but letters — and a useful conversation.
scriptures: Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
Gal 5:26
Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
corruption_summary: Mod culture made fashion the self and style a tribe; Scripture places worth in the hidden man of the heart and asks for apparel that is modest, not merely modern.
corruption_paragraphs: The Mods were the first youth subculture built almost entirely on consumption. To be a Mod was to buy the right suit, the right scooter, the right records, and to spend every penny of a working-class wage on looking sharp. The Rockers defined themselves the same way with leather and motorcycles. When the two tribes fought on the beaches in 1964, the newspapers were shocked; Paul would not have been (Gal 5:26). Identity sought in things is always fragile, and fragile identities fight.

The mod style that crossed the Atlantic brought the miniskirt, and with it a revolution in what was considered acceptable for women to wear. A Christian family need not be stuck in 1955 to see that 1Ti 2:9 still speaks. Modesty is not a fashion; it is a disposition of the heart toward God and neighbor that shows itself in dress. The modern question is always the same as the ancient one: who am I dressing for?
roots_summary: Latin modo (just now) → modernus → English modern → late-1950s London modernist (jazz fan) → 1960s Mod subculture → US mod (fashionable, 1965–67).
roots_lines: Latin modo — just now; modernus — of the present time
English modern — of the present age; new-fashioned (1828: "late; recent")
Late 1950s London: modernists — fans of modern jazz
1964: Mods and Rockers clash at Clacton, Margate, Brighton
1965–67 US: mod — Carnaby Street / Swinging London style
usage: "Grandma had a mod dress in 1966. She says her father made her wear a coat over it to church."
Let it be the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4).
Modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety (1Ti 2:9).

etymology: From French à gogo, "in abundance, galore," by way of the Paris nightclub Whisky à Go-Go (1947) and especially the Whisky a Go Go on the Sunset Strip, Los Angeles (opened January 1964), where young women danced in suspended cages above the floor. By 1965 go-go dancer, go-go girl, and go-go boots (popularized by designer André Courrèges, 1964, and Nancy Sinatra’s "These Boots Are Made for Walkin’," 1966) were national words. Separately, go-go described the booming, high-risk stock market of the late 1960s ("the go-go years") and later a Washington, D.C., funk style (1970s).
biblical_def: Go-go in the 1960s meant lively, energetic, swinging — and above all it named the go-go dancer: a young woman in a short skirt and white boots dancing in a cage or on a platform in a nightclub to entertain the crowd. The go-go boot outlived the cage and became a fashion staple. The Christian observation: Scripture loves dancing and does not love this kind. David "danced before the LORD with all his might" (2Sa 6:14); there is "a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4); Miriam led the women with timbrels after the Red Sea. Dancing for joy before God and among His people is a gift. But Scripture also records another kind of dance: "when Herod’s birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod" (Mat 14:6), and a prophet’s head was the price. The go-go cage was the Herod’s-birthday kind: a young woman put on display to please the eyes of men. Isaiah describes the daughters of Zion who "walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go" (Isa 3:16), and Proverbs warns a young man of the woman "with the attire of an harlot" (Pro 7:10). A father can tell his daughter that her body is not a show, and his son that he must not buy a ticket to one. The joy of motion belongs to worship, celebration, and marriage — not to a cage over a bar.
webster_summary: 1960s slang (French à gogo; Whisky a Go Go, 1964) for lively, swinging — above all the go-go dancer displayed for a crowd — the Herod’s-birthday dance (Mat 14:6) set against the joyful dancing of 2Sa 6:14.
webster_full: GO-GO, adj. (Boomer slang, 1964–) Lively, energetic, swinging; of a nightclub, featuring dancers. n. Go-go dancer / go-go girl — a woman employed to dance, often in a cage or on a platform, to entertain patrons. Go-go boots — white, low-heeled, calf-high boots.

Webster (1828) — GO, verb intransitive preterit tense went; participle passive gone. 1. In a general sense, to move; to pass; to proceed from one place, state or station to another; opposed to resting. A mill goes by water or by steam; a ship goes at the rate of five knots an hour; a clock goes fast or slow; a horse goes lame; a fowl or a ball goes with velocity through the air. The mourners go about the streets. Ecclesiastes 12:5 . 2. To walk; to move on the feet or step by step. The child begins to go alone at a year old. You know that love Will creep in service where it cannot go 3. To walk leisurely; not to run. Thou must run to him; for thou hast staid so long that going will scarce serve the turn.
Other senses: go-go stocks / years (speculative late-1960s market); go-go music (Washington, D.C., funk, 1970s–).
scriptures: And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod.
Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
Mat 14:6
But when Herod's birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod.
Isa 3:16
Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:
Pro 7:10
And, behold, there met him a woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart.
corruption_summary: Go-go culture turned dance into display and young women into entertainment for men; Scripture honors dancing for joy before God and condemns the dance that pleases Herod.
corruption_paragraphs: The go-go craze was marketed as fun — bright colors, boots, the Watusi and the Frug — and much of it was innocent teen dancing. But the word’s center was the nightclub cage, and the cage was a frank piece of commerce: a woman on display to sell drinks to men. It was a step on the road from the 1950s dance floor to the strip club, and the 1960s took that road quickly. Scripture’s word for that display is in Isa 3:16 and Pro 7:10, and its most chilling example is Mat 14:6.

Christian families need not be afraid of dancing. David danced before the ark, and the Song of Solomon delights in the beauty of the beloved within marriage. The line Scripture draws is not between motion and stillness but between joy offered to God and a body offered to the gaze. A wedding reception where grandparents dance with their grandchildren is closer to 2Sa 6:14 than any club ever built.
roots_summary: French à gogo (galore) → Whisky à Go-Go (Paris, 1947) → Whisky a Go Go (Los Angeles, 1964) → go-go dancer, go-go boots (1965); go-go stocks (late 1960s).
roots_lines: French à gogo — in abundance, galore (from Old French gogue, merriment)
1947: Whisky à Go-Go, Paris
January 1964: Whisky a Go Go, Sunset Strip, Los Angeles; caged dancers
1964–66: Courrèges boots; "These Boots Are Made for Walkin’" (1966)
Late 1960s: the "go-go years" of speculative stock trading
usage: "Grandma’s white go-go boots are still in the attic. She says they were for school dances, not cages, thank you very much."
David danced before the LORD with all his might (2Sa 6:14).
The daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod (Mat 14:6).

etymology: Fox, an attractive young woman, is African-American slang from the early twentieth century, mainstream by the 1960s (foxy, 1960s–70s; Jimi Hendrix’s "Foxy Lady," 1967). The intensifier stone — "completely, utterly," as in stone cold, stone crazy, stone deaf — is old English, revived in 1960s Black and hippie slang. Stone fox, a strikingly beautiful woman, was common in the late 1960s and 1970s.
biblical_def: A stone fox is a strikingly beautiful woman — the highest compliment a 1970s man could pay a woman’s looks. The grandparents’ version of today’s baddie. The Christian observation: Scripture does not pretend beauty is unimportant. It calls Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Abigail, and Esther fair, and the Song of Solomon has a husband say to his bride, "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee" (Son 4:7). In marriage, a man’s delight in his wife’s beauty is holy. But the slang ranks women by their looks and puts them on display for any man’s appraisal, and Scripture refuses that ranking. "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (Pro 31:30). The adornment God values is "the hidden man of the heart ... even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price" (1Pe 3:4). And Scripture speaks directly to the man doing the looking. "Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids" (Pro 6:25). Our Lord went further: "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mat 5:28). Job’s resolution is the godly man’s: "I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?" (Job 31:1). A grandfather who calls Grandma a stone fox after fifty years of marriage is using the word as the Song does. A young man who calls a stranger one is being asked by Scripture where his eyes are going.
webster_summary: Late-1960s–70s slang (fox, an attractive woman, + intensifier stone) for a strikingly beautiful woman — a beauty Scripture celebrates within marriage (Son 4:7) but ranks below the fear of the LORD (Pro 31:30), and guards from the lustful eye (Mat 5:28).
webster_full: STONE FOX, n. (Boomer slang, late 1960s–70s) A very attractive woman. From fox (an attractive woman; AAVE, early 20th c.) + stone (completely, utterly). Compare foxy, foxy lady.

Webster (1828) — FOX, noun 1. An animal of the genus Canis, with a straight tail, yellowish or straw-colored hair, and erect ears. This animal burrows in the earth, is remarkable for his cunning, and preys on lambs, geese, hens or other small animals. 2. A sly, cunning fellow. 3. In seaman’s language, a seizing made by twisting several rope-yarns together.
Decode for families: the 1970s stone fox is the 2020s baddie; the same counsel applies to both.
scriptures: Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Pro 6:25
Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids.
Mat 5:28
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.
Job 31:1
I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?
Son 4:7
Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.
corruption_summary: Stone fox ranks women by their looks and invites every man’s appraisal; Scripture celebrates beauty within marriage, ranks the fear of the LORD above it, and binds the eyes of men by covenant.
corruption_paragraphs: Notice the animal in the word. A fox is a prize to be hunted, admired for its sleekness, and chased. The slang made women quarry and men hunters, and the sexual revolution that ran alongside it made the hunt respectable. Many marriages of that generation were wrecked by men who never stopped looking for the next stone fox. Proverbs 6 is a long warning against exactly that, and it ends at the grave.

Scripture’s alternative is not to pretend beauty does not exist; it is to put beauty in its place. In marriage, a husband should delight in his wife — the Song of Solomon is in the Bible on purpose. Outside of it, a man makes a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1). And everywhere, the woman most worth admiring is the one who fears the LORD (Pro 31:30), whose beauty does not fade with the years because it was never only skin.
roots_summary: Old English fox + early-20th-c. AAVE fox (an attractive woman) + intensifier stone (utterly) → late-1960s–70s stone fox.
roots_lines: Old English fox — the animal; figuratively a crafty person (Luk 13:32, "that fox")
Early 20th c. AAVE: fox — an attractive young woman
1960s–70s: foxy; "Foxy Lady" (Hendrix, 1967)
Intensifier stone — completely (stone dead, stone cold), revived in 1960s slang
Late 1960s–70s: stone fox
usage: "Grandpa still calls Grandma a stone fox. She rolls her eyes and smiles every time."
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised (Pro 31:30).
I made a covenant with mine eyes (Job 31:1).
